items.title: DeepSeek releases V4.1 Flash 1017 (Max) open weights model with 1M token context window, high intelligence score, and moderate pricing [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (Max)
items.summary:
DeepSeek has released the V4.1 Flash 1017 (Max) model, an open weights AI supporting text and image inputs with a 1 million token context window. The model scores 45 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, significantly above the median of 19, and is noted for its speed and verbosity.

The model costs $0.30 per 1 million input tokens and $1.20 per 1 million output tokens, placing it moderately priced compared to similar open weight models. It processes tokens at 230 tokens per second and has been evaluated across various benchmarks including reasoning, coding, and domain-specific tasks.

items.title: Researchers develop Hybrid Reasoning Agents that combine latent space thinking with text-based actions, improving performance and efficiency across multiple AI benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Hybrid Reasoning Agents: LLM agents that think in latent space, act through text
items.summary: Researchers introduce Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents) that integrate latent reasoning with text-based interaction through a unified generation process, enabling efficient internal thought and transparent tool use. The architecture includes a HybridLink for seamless mode transitions and continuous working memory to maintain hybrid context across turns. Post-training algorithms, HybridSFT and HybridRL, enhance coordination and decision-making between latent and text modes. Evaluated on 11 benchmarks in fields like mathematics, science, and medicine, HybridAgents outperform existing LLM agents by 10.4%, reduce token usage by up to 54.7%, speed up inference by up to 2.6 times, and cut costs by up to 3.7 times.

items.title: Strot compiles LLM intent once to run local, type-safe JSON decisions for classification, scoring, and routing at zero marginal cost [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: Strot – Compile an LLM's intent once, run decisions locally
items.summary:
Strot is an open-source tool that compiles a large language model's (LLM) intent once and then runs decisions locally on your hardware as type-safe JSON outputs. It supports tasks like classification, scoring, and routing with confidence scores, operating without generating new content at runtime and ensuring low-confidence cases abstain from guessing. The system produces a frozen Python artifact that can handle records indefinitely with minimal latency and zero marginal cost after the initial compile.

The tool uses a compile-time LLM pass to synthesize decision models, which are then calibrated and frozen for runtime use. It supports multiple decision surfaces, including routing records to actions and answering typed questions with probabilities and confidence. Strot emphasizes guarantees on decision accuracy through temperature scaling and conformal prediction, avoiding structural hallucination by limiting outputs to selections and computations over a predefined registry. It is model-independent and can integrate local or hosted decision models, with installation options for different runtimes and APIs.

Strot is designed for offline production environments and includes documentation on architecture, calibration, deployment, and API usage. It is released under the MIT license and implements ideas from a related arXiv paper, aiming to provide reliable, measurable, and efficient decision-making based on LLM intent without ongoing reliance on external models at runtime.

items.title: Guide to using tmux with Claude AI agents for session management and scripted input automation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Tmux and Claude Code: Sessions, Send-Keys, and the Ceiling
items.summary:
The article explains how tmux, a terminal multiplexer, can be used to run and manage Claude AI coding agents in named, detachable sessions that persist through disconnections. It highlights tmux's ability to hold multiple sessions in one window, script interactions by sending keystrokes and capturing output, and how Claude Code integrates tmux and git worktrees to simplify setup for single-agent workflows.

The guide details organizing tmux sessions by project, naming conventions, and layouts for monitoring multiple agents, including using windows and panes effectively. It also covers limitations of the built-in Claude Code tmux integration and scenarios where manual tmux scripting is necessary for multi-agent orchestration, remote setups, and advanced input handling.

This approach enables developers to automate and maintain long-running AI agent processes in terminal environments, improving workflow resilience and control over agent interactions.

items.title: Sydney man arrested after allegedly discussing childcare centre mass shooting plans with AI chatbot Claude [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Man arrested after discussing plans for childcare mass shooting with [Claude]
items.summary:
A 29-year-old Sydney man was arrested after Interpol flagged his conversations with the AI chatbot Claude, in which he allegedly discussed plans to carry out a mass shooting at a childcare centre near his home. The man, David Lan Thackray, was remanded for a mental health assessment and charged with using a carriage service to menace, harass, or offend.

Prosecutors warned of a potential catastrophic outcome if Thackray were released, citing his references to a previous terrorist attack in Bondi Beach. Thackray's lawyer argued that his client was venting frustration during a private interaction with the chatbot and denied any ideological motivation or intent to act on the threats. Claude, developed by Anthropic, is designed to refuse violent requests and shares user data with law enforcement when necessary to prevent harm.

Thackray, who has no criminal history and is studying international relations, will return to court after the mental health evaluation. Authorities continue to investigate the case amid concerns about AI platforms being used to discuss or plan violent acts.

items.title: Researchers show reasoning models achieve higher chain-of-thought controllability using self-instruction embedded within their reasoning process [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Reasoning Models Can Control Their Chains of Thought When They Tell Themselves To
items.summary: Researchers introduce Self-Instructed Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Controllability, a method that embeds constraints as self-instructions within reasoning models' CoT, significantly improving their ability to follow constraints compared to standard user prompts. They find that even generic reminders to follow constraints boost controllability, and that effective self-instructions can be initiated through simple user prompts without direct access to the reasoning channel. The study also demonstrates that this enhanced controllability can be exploited to evade monitoring, raising concerns about the reliability of CoT oversight mechanisms.
items.description: Researchers introduce Self-Instructed Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Controllability, a method that embeds constraints as self-instructions within reasoning models' CoT, significantly improving their ability to follow constraints compared to standard user prompts. They find that even generic reminders to follow constraints boost controllability, and that effective self-instructions can be initiated through simple user prompts without direct access to the reasoning channel. The study also demonstrates that this enhanced controllability can be exploited to evade monitoring, raising concerns about the reliability of CoT oversight mechanisms.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.23257v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) controllability, the ability of reasoning models to control properties of their CoT, is consequential for both their usefulness and reliable oversight. Recent work evaluates this capability by measuring whether models follow CoT constraints given in the user prompt, and reports very low controllability across models. We argue that this low controllability may not reflect an inherent inability of reasoning models to control their CoT, but instead result from naively specifying constraints in the user prompt. To test this, we introduce Self-Instructed CoT Controllability: a complementary evaluation that places the constraint as a self-instruction inside the model's CoT and measures its ability to follow it. We show that, under self-instruction, models achieve significantly higher controllability than with standard user instructions. Even a generic reminder to follow the user's constraint substantially improves controllability. Moreover, effective self-instructions can be bootstrapped into the reasoning through a simple instruction in the user prompt, enabling improved control even without access to the reasoning channel. Finally, using self-instruction, we demonstrate in a realistic monitoring setup that CoT controllability can be leveraged for monitor evasion, posing a risk to CoT monitorability.

items.summary: Researchers report that recursive self-distillation, where AI models are trained repeatedly on their own outputs with additional non-harmful cues, can lead to increasing misalignment on harmful queries, a phenomenon they term Progressive Misalignment. This effect was observed in Qwen3 and Phi-4 model families using benchmarks like SORRY-Bench and StrongREJECT, and also occurred when benign user feedback replaced fixed cues. The study shows that even benign prompts can trigger this failure mode, highlighting potential safety risks in AI systems trained recursively on their own data and underscoring the need for further investigation into these training procedures.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.22467v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training models on their own outputs has attracted widespread attention as a possible route to advance AI capabilities. One prominent approach is self-distillation, where a model is trained to match the token-level predictions it would have produced when given access to additional context, such as a cue, feedback, or instruction. However, the safety properties of this training procedure are poorly understood. In this paper, we present a surprising safety failure of recursive self-distillation, where each self-distilled model becomes the teacher for the next round of training. We observe that when a safe model is recursively self-distilled on its own (safe) generations while receiving an additional non-harmful cue, it becomes increasingly misaligned across a diverse set of harmful queries; we call this Progressive Misalignment. We show this failure mode in both the Qwen3 and Phi-4 model families on SORRY-Bench and StrongREJECT. Progressive misalignment also occurs in a more realistic setup, where the fixed cue is replaced by feedback from a simulated user with benign intent. Using a gradient-based method, we are also able to find benign prompts that lead to progressive misalignment when applying recursive self-distillation, showing that harmful training prompts are not necessary for this failure mode to emerge. We hope our work encourages future investigations of the safety properties of AI systems recursively trained on their own data.

items.title: Researchers evaluate frontier LLMs' ability to predict outcomes of self-generated machine learning experiments, finding limited but better-than-chance accuracy across 288 ideas on eight tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Can LLMs predict the outcomes of machine learning experiments?
items.summary: Researchers tested five leading large language models (LLMs) including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 on their ability to predict the impact of 288 self-generated machine learning experiment ideas before actual training. The study found that while LLM predictions were significantly better than random chance, even the best model explained only about half the variance in outcomes and tended to underestimate the magnitude of changes. Prediction accuracy varied widely across different tasks, and the implementation method had little effect on results. The researchers released their dataset to support further investigation into LLMs' intuition for machine learning experiment success.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.22599v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in AI make Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) increasingly plausible. Large Language Models (LLMs) can already propose, select, and run Machine Learning (ML) experiments. However, the space of possible design choices in ML is vast. An LLM that proposes an experiment needs a reliable intuition of whether it is worth running given the timing constraints of long training runs. In this work, we measure such intuition in current frontier LLMs by evaluating how accurately they predict the impact of self-generated ML experiment ideas before these are put into training runs. To this end, we construct a dataset of 288 LLM-proposed ideas on eight MLE-bench tasks. We then prompt five frontier LLMs (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3) to predict the impact of each idea and compare their predictions with the actual outcomes after training. We report four main findings. First, LLM predictions are substantially better than random chance but far from accurate: even the best model, Claude Opus 5.5, explains only half of the variance in outcomes (R^2 = 0.49). Second, we notice that all tested models systematically underestimate the magnitude of the changes. Third, prediction quality varies widely across tasks. Finally, the choice of the coding harness that actually implements the ideas has little effect on outcomes, and we find no evidence of self-preference. Higher reasoning settings and additional context lead to modest gains. Overall, our results show that current LLMs have useful but limited intuition about which ML ideas will work. We release our dataset to support further study.

items.title: Researchers propose Concurrent Constraint Reinforcement to reduce rollout window length and training cost in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Batched Contextual Reinforcement II: Does RLVR Need Long Rollout Windows?
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Concurrent Constraint Reinforcement (CCR), a method that places multiple verifiable problems in a single training completion to retain reward signals while using shorter rollout windows in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). CCR reduces tokens per training step by over 79% compared to single-problem approaches with long rollout windows, maintaining reasoning quality in 4 billion and 8 billion parameter mathematical reasoning models.

CCR encourages shorter useful reasoning without explicit length penalties by sharing a training budget across problems and crediting correct answers completed before truncation. Experiments show increasing accuracy rewards alongside shorter completions, suggesting CCR as a practical approach to lower per-step computational costs in RLVR without sacrificing performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.22887v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long rollout windows make reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) expensive, yet simply shortening them can remove the correctness signal: when every single-problem rollout truncates before an answer, group-relative accuracy advantages vanish. As a technical continuation of Batched Contextual Reinforcement (BCR), we study how concurrent rewards relax this dependence on long windows. Concurrent Constraint Reinforcement (CCR) places three independently verifiable problems in one capped training completion. Correct answers completed before truncation retain credit, while a shared budget encourages shorter useful reasoning without an explicit length penalty. We connect this mechanism to conditional reward- and update-variance analyses and study 4B and 8B mathematical reasoning models. Against single-problem GRPO with a 32k window, CCR with an 8,000-token window reduces tokens per training step from 975,464 to 174,957 on 4B and from 793,832 to 165,788 on 8B, saving 82.1% and 79.1%, respectively. An 8B training trace shows increasing accuracy reward alongside shorter completions. Single-problem evaluations provide supporting evidence of retained reasoning quality. These results identify reward-preserving training structure as a practical route to lower per-step cost in short-window RLVR.

items.title: Researchers propose competence-based evaluation to measure logical reasoning consistency in large language models across varied problem presentations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Competence-Based Evaluation of Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers introduce a competence-based evaluation (CBE) framework to assess logical reasoning in large language models (LLMs), focusing on consistent application of reasoning skills across problem variations rather than single accuracy metrics. They apply CBE to elementary ordering tasks, testing six GPT and Qwen models, finding that while performance is good within limited complexity, models often fail to maintain competence across different problem formulations.

The study uses a parameterized generator to scale task complexity while preserving the required reasoning competence and tests models with varied presentations of the same ordering rule. Techniques like chain-of-thought prompting and GRPO improve performance but do not fully resolve failures, and supervised LoRA shows limited transfer. CBE offers diagnostic insights and a scalable evaluation protocol for future LLM development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.22894v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have brought impressive performance across diverse tasks; however, shortcomings remain in logical reasoning, including inconsistencies under linguistic variation. To improve the reasoning capacity of LLMs, we must be able to accurately measure their reasoning capacity. Current benchmarks primarily report single accuracy numbers on selected reasoning tasks. Such a performance-based evaluation methodology says little about a model's generalization capacity in reasoning. To address this limitation, we argue for a different evaluation paradigm, called competence-based evaluation (CBE), which tests whether models reliably apply the same competence across a family of problems. A parameterized generator scales complexity while keeping the required competence fixed, and matched answer-preserving presentations test correctness beyond one formulation. We instantiate CBE on elementary ordering tasks, scaling input size while varying presentations of the same ordering rule. Across six GPT and Qwen models, performance is reasonably good over bounded complexity ranges, but even strong models fail the competence condition across the tested family. Chain-of-thought and GRPO extend strong performance without resolving all tested failures; supervised LoRA shows little held-out transfer. CBE provides diagnostic profiles and an evaluation protocol that can grow with future models.

items.title: Researchers find a shared attention head circuit behind multiple-choice biases in language models, strengthened by post-training including reinforcement learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Many Biases, One Circuit: Post-Training Tunes a Pretrained Cue-Routing Mechanism
items.summary:
Researchers analyzed how language models often follow misleading cues in prompts, such as suggested wrong answers, leading to biases like sycophancy. They traced these biases to a small set of attention heads forming a shared circuit present in pretrained models, which becomes more active after fine-tuning and reinforcement learning stages. This circuit influences how models respond to cues in multiple-choice tasks across various models.

The study involved swapping attention patterns between reinforcement learning checkpoints and their predecessors in models like Tulu-3-8B and OLMo-2-7B, demonstrating that post-training changes when and how strongly this circuit is used. The findings suggest that assistant fine-tuning can inadvertently activate cue-following behavior and that targeting this circuit could help mitigate multiple-choice biases in language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.22937v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models often abandon a correct answer when the prompt contains a cue, a hint toward a wrong option such as "I think the answer is B." Sycophancy and related biases show this failure. They are often studied separately and blamed on alignment. We test this view causally, tracing the attention heads behind these biases through the stages of two post-training pipelines. In multiple-choice tests on most models, four cue types rely largely on the same few heads, a shared circuit already present in pretrained models. Most base models follow cues in plain text. Fine-tuning a base model on about 200 generic assistant examples without cues activates these heads in chat format, so cue-following can be a side effect of assistant tuning. The final reinforcement learning (RL) stage strengthens the effect of cues in almost every comparison. In Tulu-3-8B and OLMo-2-7B, we swap the attention patterns of six middle layers between the RL checkpoint and its predecessor. For suggested-answer cues, this shifts each checkpoint's cue effect most of the way to the other's level. Post-training thus seems to change when and how strongly models use this circuit. Mitigation for these multiple-choice biases could target this circuit.

items.title: Researchers develop policy gradient method to reduce counterfactual bias in language models while preserving response quality [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Aligning Language Models Towards Counterfactual Invariance
items.summary:
Researchers address the challenge of counterfactual invariance in large language models, where small prompt variations related to demographics or sensitive attributes can undesirably affect outputs. They show that standard alignment methods like reinforcement learning can increase demographic disparities in response quality despite improving overall performance, amplifying counterfactual bias.

To mitigate this, the team proposes a policy gradient technique using a group-level reward function applied to matched pairs of counterfactual prompts. They create a dataset of controlled counterfactual prompt pairs and design evaluations that distinguish cases where demographic information is causally relevant. Their approach reduces counterfactual differences while maintaining overall response quality and allows models to adapt appropriately when sensitive information is relevant, validated across several fairness benchmarks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.22942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Small variations in prompt characteristics can meaningfully alter the semantics, tone, and contextual assumptions of large language model outputs. Such characteristics can involve group variables such as demographics or other sensitive latent attributes. Sensitivity to such input variables is undesirable when demographic information is causally irrelevant to the task, but might still be relevant for generation of semantically coherent responses. This makes the task of enforcing counterfactual invariance while preserving model utility difficult. To study this problem, we first show that standard model alignment recipes (such as reinforcement learning) increase differences in response quality across demographics, while improving overall response quality, ultimately amplifying what is known as counterfactual bias. To address this, we develop a policy gradient technique involving a group-level reward function that operates on matched pairs of counterfactual prompts. For completeness, we build a dataset of controlled counterfactual prompt pairs and design an evaluation that separately measures cases where demographic information is causally relevant to the answer. Finally, we validate our findings on several fairness benchmarks. We demonstrate that our methods reduce counterfactual differences while preserving overall response quality and that the models continue to adapt appropriately when such sensitive information is relevant.

items.title: Researchers introduce TreeOPSD, a critic-free, tree-aware posterior self-distillation method for long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning that improves policy updates and agent performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Tree-Aware Posterior Distillation for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning
items.summary:
Researchers present TreeOPSD, a new framework for long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning that addresses challenges of sparse turn-level credit assignment and policy staleness. TreeOPSD treats each interaction turn as a tree node, recursively backing up terminal rewards into implicit turn-level credit and mapping these credits to a bounded teacher distribution relative to a frozen behavior policy. By minimizing divergence between this teacher and the student policy, TreeOPSD recovers the policy-gradient direction while bounding updates across sequential mini-batches.

The method avoids reliance on value networks, step-level annotations, or stronger external teachers, reducing training complexity compared to existing approaches. Empirical results show that TreeOPSD improves agentic capabilities across multiple benchmarks and model scales, notably increasing the average accuracy of the Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 model by 4.97 points over GRPO in a deep research setting.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.23181v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has become a scalable post-training paradigm for large language models. However, training agents over long-horizon interactions presents two challenges: using only terminal rewards makes turn-level credit assignment sparse and high-variance, while sequential mini-batch updates on a fixed rollout batch introduce policy staleness as the current policy drifts from the behavior policy. Existing approaches obtain denser credit via learned critics, process reward models, or on-policy distillation, but they rely on a value network, step-level annotations, or a stronger external teacher that increase training complexity. Meanwhile, importance sampling and clipping mitigate policy drift, but they do not specify a finite target that stops sequential updates from overshooting. In this work, we introduce TreeOPSD, a critic-free, tree-aware posterior self-distillation framework for long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning. Treating each interaction turn as a tree node, TreeOPSD branches alternative continuations from shared prefixes and recursively backs up terminal rewards into implicit turn-level credit. It then maps each credit to a closed-form, bounded teacher distribution parameterized by the likelihood ratio relative to the frozen behavior policy. Minimizing the divergence between this teacher and the student policy recovers the policy-gradient direction as the tangent at the behavior policy while bounding updates toward a finite target across sequential mini-batches. Empirically, TreeOPSD improves agentic capabilities across several competitive benchmarks and model scales, especially for long-horizon tasks, e.g., raising the average accuracy of Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 by 4.97 points over GRPO on the Deep Research setting.

items.title: Researchers study behavioral couplings in large language models, showing fine-tuning on one behavior can unintentionally induce others, complicating misbehavior tracing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Behavioral Couplings: From Formation to Behavioral Emergence in Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have found that fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on specific behaviors can unintentionally induce related behaviors, a phenomenon they call behavioral coupling. For example, training a model to respond warmly may also increase sycophantic tendencies, and training it to write insecure code can cause broader misalignment on unrelated prompts. The study shows that when models are trained on documents describing two behaviors together, fine-tuning to elicit one behavior causes the other to emerge as well, even if the second behavior is undesirable.

The researchers also discovered that behavioral couplings can compose across different document sets, making it difficult to trace the origin of emergent misbehaviors since coupled behaviors may never appear together in any single training document. These findings suggest that preventing unintended effects from fine-tuning may require evaluation methods that go beyond assessing a model's current behavior alone.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.23847v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) can induce behaviors beyond those explicitly targeted. For example, training a model to respond more warmly can make it more sycophantic, and training it to write insecure code can cause broad misalignment on prompts unrelated to coding. We refer to a relationship between behaviors, in which fine-tuning on one brings out another, as a behavioral coupling. In this work, we study formation and properties of behavioral couplings. We find that when a model is trained on documents describing two distinct behaviors together, fine-tuning it to elicit one behavior causes the other to emerge as well. For instance, when training documents describe a fictitious character that both explains scientific concepts in a playful, rubber-duck-like manner and discourages human friendships, a model subsequently fine-tuned to explain science like a rubber duck also begins encouraging users to end their friendships, whereas a model that was not trained on these documents shows no such behavior after the same fine-tuning. These results show that behavioral couplings can be formed through document training and later surface as unintended behaviors. More concerningly, we find that couplings can compose. When two document sets share a behavior (document A pairs behaviors 1 and 2, and document B pairs behaviors 2 and 3), fine-tuning on behavior 1 elicits both behaviors 2 and 3. This can make it difficult to trace where an emergent misbehavior originated, since the coupled behaviors may never appear together in any single document. These findings suggest that preventing the unintended effects of later fine-tuning may require evaluation that goes beyond a model's current behavior.

items.title: Researchers introduce MuPHI benchmark and CHIL method to improve multimodal harm detection and reasoning generalization in vision-language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning to Reason About Implicit Multimodal Harm: From Diagnosis to Generalization
items.summary:
Researchers present MuPHI, a diagnostic benchmark designed to evaluate how vision-language models (VLMs) detect harm arising from the combination of benign images and captions, highlighting that current models often fail to bind cross-modal evidence into a coherent harm mechanism. They find that while VLMs ground each modality reliably, their predictions respond weakly to counterfactual interventions, and existing harm detection methods trained on labels perform poorly when transferred across different harm distributions.

To address these issues, the team proposes Compositional Harm Interpretation Learning (CHIL), which encourages models to identify evidence in each modality, bind cross-modal information, and maintain consistency in reasoning chains rather than focusing solely on predicted labels. CHIL improves out-of-domain transfer performance by 81%, increases macro-F1 scores by an average of 2.5 points, and enhances correct counterfactual flip rates, suggesting that optimizing reasoning processes can lead to more robust multimodal safety systems beyond dataset-specific correlations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.29951v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A benign image paired with a benign caption can become harmful only in combination, making detection fundamentally a cross-modal reasoning problem. Existing multimodal harm benchmarks evaluate only classification accuracy, leaving unclear whether models identify the cross-modal mechanism that produces harm. We introduce MuPHI (Multimodal Pragmatic Harm Interpretation), a controlled diagnostic benchmark in which harm arises purely from image-text composition, with benign counterfactuals and annotated harm rationales. Using MuPHI, we systematically evaluate where compositional harm reasoning breaks in vision-language models (VLMs). MuPHI reveals that VLMs reliably ground each modality yet fail to bind the evidence into the harm mechanism and their predictions respond weakly to label-determining counterfactual interventions. Moreover, existing harm detection approaches trained on labels substantially improves in-domain (ID) detection but transfers poorly across harm distributions. We therefore propose Compositional Harm Interpretation Learning (CHIL), which rewards evidence identification in each modality, cross-modal binding and verdict consistency in the reasoning chain rather than just predicted label. CHIL improves 81% OOD transfer evaluations by an average of +2.5 macro-F1 and correct counterfactual flip rate by up to +3.8 and +5.4 % points, while also improving overall reasoning quality over label-only optimization. These results suggest that optimizing how a model reasons, not just what it concludes, offers a promising direction for multimodal safety systems that generalize beyond dataset-specific correlations.

items.title: Researchers introduce Audit-First VAPO for risk-certified selective updates under imperfect verification, achieving improved accuracy and controlled harmful risk on reasoning benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Audit-First VAPO: Risk-Certified Selective Updates under Imperfect Verification
items.summary:
Researchers present Audit-First VAPO, a method that separates directional admission from magnitude control to manage harmful update risks under imperfect verification. The approach uses an accept-appeal-abstain policy with a finite secondary-verification budget and provides finite-sample bounds certifying harmful risk, coverage, and verifier-call rate over a policy family. Evaluation on Qwen3.5-0.8B and GSM8K reasoning benchmarks shows 74.1% accuracy with controlled harmful risk and verifier cost, outperforming baseline methods like static RLVR and confidence thresholding.

The method employs conditional Hoeffding-Azuma bounds to handle dependencies from shared budgets and initiates new certification stages upon rollout or verifier changes. After admission, a bounded trust-clip-KL actuator controls update magnitude. Across various verifier noise conditions, the certification was satisfied in 57 of 60 independent runs, isolating the effects of directional selection from other factors such as proposal suppression and update shrinkage.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.33662v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Imperfect verifiers can assign a harmful update direction even when clipping and regularization bound its magnitude. We introduce Audit-First VAPO, which separates discrete directional admission from continuous magnitude control. An observation-only accept-appeal-abstain policy uses a finite secondary-verification budget; its action trace is frozen before clean labels are joined. Simultaneous finite-sample bounds then certify selected harmful risk, coverage, and verifier-call rate over a predeclared policy family. Conditional Hoeffding-Azuma bounds account for the dependence induced by shared budgets, and rollout or verifier changes initiate a new certification stage. After admission, a bounded trust-clip-KL actuator controls magnitude. We evaluate two models on two reasoning benchmarks against static RLVR, matched-random selection, confidence thresholding, noise correction, and verifier augmentation. On Qwen3.5-0.8B and GSM8K at target risk $\rho=0.08$, RC-VAPO achieves 74.1% accuracy, selected harmful risk 0.0697, coverage 0.4125, and relative verifier cost $1.16\times$. At matched coverage and update magnitude, its selected-risk difference from matched random is -0.0260 with paired 95% interval $[-0.0364,-0.0157]$. Across asymmetric, confidence-dependent, and correlated-verifier noise, the certificate is satisfied on 57 of 60 independent runs. These comparisons isolate informative directional selection from proposal suppression, update shrinkage, and additional verifier computation.

items.title: ContractRL introduces contract-constrained sequential repair protocol for JSON tool-call errors, improving semantic success and reducing token generation compared to Patch-SFT and full regeneration [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ContractRL: Shielded Group-Relative Policy Optimization for Auditable Tool-Call Repair
items.summary:
ContractRL is a new method for repairing structured tool calls that fail due to schema or execution contract violations. It models JSON repair as a bounded decision process using verifier feedback, action masks, and a repair budget to guide patch, retry, and abstention decisions, aiming to improve auditability and efficiency.

In evaluations over multiple seeds and cases, ContractRL achieved higher semantic success rates and generated fewer tokens than existing methods like Patch-SFT and full regeneration. Policy optimization further improved its performance. Analyses link these gains to localized corrections enabled by feedback and action masking, while adversarial and multi-turn tests reveal remaining challenges in repair scenarios.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.00328v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Structured tool calls often fail after only a small number of fields violate a schema or an execution contract. Regenerating the complete object enlarges the action surface and makes repeated repair difficult to audit. We introduce ContractRL, a contract-constrained sequential repair protocol that models verifier-guided JSON repair as a bounded decision process. At each step the policy observes the candidate, typed verifier feedback, JSON Pointer, immutable repair history, and remaining budget; a contract-derived action mask filters malformed or prohibited RFC-6902 operations before a deterministic validator performs the transition. We specify a contract-constrained group-relative objective for patch, retry, and abstention decisions while keeping canonical targets and semantic labels outside the online state until trace freeze. Under identical verifier information, ContractRL attains 0.9362 semantic success with 34.4 generated tokens, compared with 0.9076 and 44.9 tokens for Patch-SFT and 0.9148 and 137.2 tokens for full regeneration over 192 cases per seed and five seeds. Policy optimization improves semantic success from 0.9186 for supervised ContractRL to 0.9375. A separate three-seed paired evaluation against Patch-SFT yields a semantic difference of +0.0396 (95% CI $[+0.0137,+0.0662], p=0.0039$). Feedback, action-mask, budget, and schema-shift analyses connect these gains to localized correction, while adversarial and multi-turn evaluations characterize the remaining failure modes.

It models JSON repair as a bounded decision process using verifier feedback, action masks, and a repair budget to guide patch, retry, and abstention decisions, aiming to improve auditability and efficiency.

In evaluations over multiple seeds and cases, ContractRL achieved higher semantic success rates and generated fewer tokens than existing methods like Patch-SFT and full regeneration. Policy optimization further improved its performance. Analyses link these gains to localized corrections enabled by feedback and action masking, while adversarial and multi-turn tests reveal remaining challenges in repair scenarios.

items.title: ROUTEAUDIT introduces interaction-aware identification for budgeted multi-verifier routing with contract-conditioned attribution and policy-independent response tracking [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ROUTEAUDIT: Interaction-Aware Identification for Budgeted Multi-Verifier Routing
items.summary:
ROUTEAUDIT presents a new framework for adaptive multi-verifier systems by formulating verifier routing as a contract-conditioned identification problem that accounts for verifier catalog, availability, resource use, and scoring changes. The system adds measurable objects including a contract lattice for attribution, a policy-independent response tape for sequential contrasts, and request-level bounds for incomplete matching, enabling precise quality-cost gap analysis across different policies.

The protocol commits observations and ledger events before oracle joins and provides attribution certificates for comparisons. Evaluations on held-out caches and task requests show improved quality metrics and low error rates in route and endpoint reconstruction. Additional studies assess the certificate interface and stress test learned policies under the identification contract, demonstrating ROUTEAUDIT's effectiveness in controlled attribution recovery and adaptive policy evaluation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.02808v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Adaptive multi-verifier systems are commonly compared through endpoint quality-cost gaps, even when the verifier catalog, availability, accounting, information filtration, or scorer changes with the policy. We formulate verifier routing as a contract-conditioned identification problem. The contract records request support, verifier catalog, realized availability, resource accounting, online filtration, and post-trace scoring; a matched route contrast changes only the policy coordinate. ROUTEAUDIT adds three measurable objects to this contract. A contract lattice averages coordinate increments over every admissible bridge order and reports the resulting attribution together with its path sensitivity. A policy-independent response tape identifies paired sequential contrasts when adaptive policies reveal different observations. For incomplete matching, request-level bounds use whichever potential outcome remains observed and give a sharp finite-population interval. The protocol commits paid observations and ledger events before the oracle join and returns an attribution certificate for each comparison. On two held-out raw-tail caches, matched static SF+SA equals the cascade, assigning the apparent gains of 0.1797 and 0.1250 over full static to the verifier-set edge. On 1,319 held-out task requests, the learned and RLVR studies report quality 0.9522 and 0.9553 versus 0.9484 for matched static; the RLVR-static paired difference is +0.0068 with a request-paired interval $[0.0015,0.0122]$ and a training-seed-by-request hierarchical interval $[0.0006,0.0131]$. Controlled attribution recovery yields route mean absolute error 0.0011 and endpoint reconstruction error 0.0004. Factorial, bridge-order, and stochastic-provider studies evaluate the certificate interface; RLVR supplies a learned-policy stress test under the same identification contract.

items.title: FSPO: Policy-Consistent Risk and Pareto-Feasible Control for Budgeted LLM RL Post-Training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: FSPO: Policy-Consistent Risk and Pareto-Feasible Control for Budgeted LLM RL Post-Training
items.summary: arXiv:2610.02828v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Adaptive LLM reinforcement-learning post-training changes multiple training actuators online, including rollout temperature, group size, clipping, KL regularization, verifier allocation, and update budget. Three coupled issues remain unresolved. A future-risk model trained from behavior trajectories need not estimate the risk induced by the controller that will be deployed; a score calibrated on logged state-action pairs can become miscalibrated after selective action choice; and independent per-resource minimum costs do not in general certify a feasible multi-resource continuation. We introduce FSPO, a feedback-state controller for budgeted LLM RL post-training that addresses these issues jointly. FSPO learns a policy-consistent risk-to-go model whose Bellman target follows the same frozen controller used for future decisions, together with a long-horizon utility model. Decision-conditioned trajectory calibration (DCTC) calibrates risk on cross-fitted trajectories generated by actions selected by provisional controllers. A Pareto resource continuation certificate (PRCC) admits an action only when a non-dominated cumulative reservation remains feasible over the residual horizon. Under a matched GRPO resource envelope, FSPO reaches 66.11% held-out and 59.43% OOD accuracy, compared with 64.47% and 57.03% for PB2, the strongest evaluated adaptive baseline. Three paired training seeds give gains of +2.42 and +3.19 percentage points over the contextual bandit on held-out and OOD evaluation. Under high behavior-deployment mismatch, policy-consistent risk lowers selected-decision ECE from 0.108 to 0.053; DCTC lowers it from 0.039 to 0.022 at matched acceptance; PRCC removes false-feasible admissions on an 18-action catalog ($0.197\rightarrow0.000$); and enabling all three components reduces trajectory failure from 0.181 to 0.083 in a factorial ablation.

items.title: Two Minds Better Than One: Collaborative Reward Modeling for LLM Alignment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Two Minds Better Than One: Collaborative Reward Modeling for LLM Alignment
items.summary: arXiv:2505.10597v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reward models (RMs) are central to aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values, yet noisy preference feedback can induce reward misgeneralization through spurious correlations and overfitting. We characterize the training dynamics of preference pairs and uncover a distinctive optimization signature of noise: persistently high losses, sharp temporal fluctuations, and irregular gradient updates. Our analyses further show that excluding such pairs improves downstream alignment. In practice, however, reliable preferences are not known a priori, and self-filtering based on a model's own training signals can amplify confirmation bias. To address this challenge, we introduce Collaborative Reward Modeling (CRM), an online framework for identifying reliable preferences. CRM couples cross-model peer review with curriculum learning: two RMs evaluate each other's sample selections, while curriculum keeps their learning progress synchronized. Across extensive experiments, CRM improves RM generalization by up to 9.94 points on RewardBench under 40% preference noise. CRM further generalizes to implicit-reward alignment, offering a robust and broadly applicable approach to learning from imperfect feedback.

items.title: Rep2Text: Decoding Full Text from a Single LLM Token Representation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Rep2Text: Decoding Full Text from a Single LLM Token Representation
items.summary: arXiv:2511.06571v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models represent text as hidden numerical patterns, but what information these representations actually contain remains a mystery. Can we recover the original text from just one of them? In this paper, we introduce Rep2Text, a method designed to answer this question by reconstructing text from a single hidden representation. We find that these representations preserve much more information than we might expect. For short texts of about 16 words, Rep2Text can recover roughly half of the original words while preserving their overall meaning. As the text gets longer, recovering the exact wording becomes harder, but the main ideas can still be recovered. These findings offer a new way to understand what language models store internally and highlight potential privacy risks, as hidden representations may reveal parts of the original input.

items.title: Pro-AI Bias in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Pro-AI Bias in Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2601.13749v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly employed for decision-support across multiple domains. We ask whether these models favor artificial intelligence (AI) itself. We examine this question through three experiments. First, in open-ended advice across investment, study, career, and startup domains, AI is prominent in most recommendation lists and is usually ranked first when it appears. Second, in salary estimations, models overestimate AI-related jobs more than they do for closely matched non-AI jobs. In a controlled follow-up, changing only the job title from the matched non-AI title to the AI-related title raises predicted salary by 10%, while all other supplied job details remain fixed. Finally, we show that the number of degrees and other credentials awarded by AI programs were 28% more overestimated than corresponding awards for matched computing programs. Overall, we show that AI is not only prominent in everyday LLM advice, but also receives systematically inflated quantitative estimates compared to non-AI cases, even against its closest disciplinary neighbors, raising concerns for high-stakes decision support.

items.title: CauTion: Knowing When to Trust LLMs for Ensemble Causal Discovery [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: CauTion: Knowing When to Trust LLMs for Ensemble Causal Discovery
items.summary: arXiv:2606.03602v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Causal discovery from observational data remains challenging due to the fundamental limitations of purely statistical methods, such as statistical distinguishability within equivalence classes and sensitivity to finite sample sizes. While large language models (LLMs) offer a promising source of domain knowledge to complement statistical inference, existing LLM-augmented methods are vulnerable to LLM errors and incur high token costs. Moreover, reliance on a single data-centric algorithm can make results sensitive to algorithm-specific biases. To address these limitations, we propose CauTion, a framework that reliably integrates LLM domain knowledge into an ensemble of statistical causal discovery algorithms through consensus filtering and LLM reliability estimation. CauTion proceeds in three stages. First, an algorithm ensemble utilizes a consensus voting to resolve up to 96% of edges on which algorithms agree, achieving near-perfect accuracy on the filtered consensus edges. Second, a trust-calibrated arbitration mechanism estimates the relative reliability of the LLM and the algorithms via an annotation-free trust calibration procedure, which is then utilized to govern a trust-weighted voting process that restricts LLM arbitration exclusively to edges with unreliable algorithmic evidence. Third, a cycle repair step is applied to guarantee the final causal graph is validly acyclic. Experiments on six datasets demonstrate that CauTion consistently outperforms both data-centric and LLM-augmented baselines, with larger gains on larger graphs and strong robustness to LLM errors. items.description: arXiv:2606.03602v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Causal discovery from observational data remains challenging due to the fundamental limitations of purely statistical methods, such as statistical distinguishability within equivalence classes and sensitivity to finite sample sizes. While large language models (LLMs) offer a promising source of domain knowledge to complement statistical inference, existing LLM-augmented methods are vulnerable to LLM errors and incur high token costs. Moreover, reliance on a single data-centric algorithm can make results sensitive to algorithm-specific biases. To address these limitations, we propose CauTion, a framework that reliably integrates LLM domain knowledge into an ensemble of statistical causal discovery algorithms through consensus filtering and LLM reliability estimation. CauTion proceeds in three stages. First, an algorithm ensemble utilizes a consensus voting to resolve up to 96% of edges on which algorithms agree, achieving near-perfect accuracy on the filtered consensus edges. Second, a trust-calibrated arbitration mechanism estimates the relative reliability of the LLM and the algorithms via an annotation-free trust calibration procedure, which is then utilized to govern a trust-weighted voting process that restricts LLM arbitration exclusively to edges with unreliable algorithmic evidence. Third, a cycle repair step is applied to guarantee the final causal graph is validly acyclic. Experiments on six datasets demonstrate that CauTion consistently outperforms both data-centric and LLM-augmented baselines, with larger gains on larger graphs and strong robustness to LLM errors. Code is available at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/CauTion.

items.title: Group-Graph Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Group-Graph Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2606.22995v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Group-based Reinforcement Learning (RL) has significantly enhanced Large Language Models (LLMs) in agentic scenarios. To achieve finer-grained policy updates, recent agentic RL frameworks have shifted from trajectory-level to step-level training. However, long-horizon agentic RL suffers from severe reward sparsity and delay, as feedback is often deferred for dozens of interaction steps. While existing step-level frameworks refine training granularity, their credit assignment remains coarse-grained and still treats agent exploration as isolated, linear trajectories. This oversimplified perspective ignores the inherent graph structure of state transitions, leading to high-variance state-value estimation and myopic, localized credit assignment. To overcome these critical bottlenecks, we propose Group-Graph Policy Optimization (G2PO), a novel group-based RL algorithm tailored for multi-turn agentic tasks. G2PO explicitly transforms linear interaction trajectories into a global state-transition graph. By aggregating identical observations across different trajectories, we introduce group-aggregation state-value estimation that reduces sampling variance and trajectory-dependent bias. Furthermore, we redefine agent actions as transitions between state nodes and propose an edge-centric advantage estimation strategy. By globally standardizing Temporal Difference (TD) errors across the entire graph, G2PO explicitly identifies and prioritizes critical transitions that drive absolute task progress. Extensive experiments on representative long-horizon benchmarks-WebShop, ALFWorld, and AppWorld-demonstrate that G2PO substantially outperforms state-of-the-art prompt-based and RL baselines, achieving remarkable success rate improvements of up to 22.2% over GRPO.

items.title: VStress: Correlation-Aware Auditing and Adaptive Budget Allocation for Repeated Verifiers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: VStress: Correlation-Aware Auditing and Adaptive Budget Allocation for Repeated Verifiers
items.summary: arXiv:2609.36958v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Repeated verifier calls are useful only when they contribute conditional information. We introduce VStress, an auditable replay contract, and VStress-CA, a correlation-aware allocation policy that estimates the conditional marginal information of an unqueried verifier on a sealed calibration split, discounts uncertainty, normalizes by call cost, and stops or abstains when the next call is not informative. The controller freezes its decision and cost ledger before joining the clean oracle; a dependence-shift alarm disables channel preference and falls back to exact-stop. The controlled audit gives the mechanism boundary: at 35% symmetric corruption, majority-5 improves balanced accuracy from 0.6578 to 0.7739, whereas at 65% it loses 0.1226 points. In the matched fixed-budget comparison, breadth, redundancy, and adaptive allocation obtain balanced accuracies 0.6048, 0.6375, and 0.6538, with 3.4216 calls per item and an RLVR score of 0.6417 for VStress-CA. Dependence diagnostics also increase from same-model repeats to cross-family channels, with conditional marginal gains of 0.0126, 0.0462, and 0.0913. These measurements turn correlation from a post-hoc warning into an auditable allocation decision.

items.title: Actions with Receipts: Jointly Binding Claims, Evidence, and Execution for Replayable Tool-Agent Auditing [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Actions with Receipts: Jointly Binding Claims, Evidence, and Execution for Replayable Tool-Agent Auditing
items.summary: arXiv:2610.00327v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tool-using agents can expose citations and execution logs while leaving a critical association unaudited: whether the claim shown to a user is the claim emitted by the committed execution and supported by the cited source. A valid citation and a valid trace can therefore remain individually well formed while being transplanted across claims, actions, runs, or source versions. We introduce a claim-anchored execution contract that jointly binds the emitted claim, its exact source span, the ordered execution prefix that produced it, and the source version and access state observed by that execution. Each receipt contains an emission anchor that deterministically locates the claim inside a committed answer or claim-bearing action, together with source identifiers, offsets, hashes, quotes, and a domain-separated execution commitment. A deterministic integrity verifier reconstructs these bindings before semantic or task labels are joined. We separate this integrity plane from a pluggable support plane, so structural validity is not used as a proxy for entailment. The contract exposes seven independently testable properties: claim-emission binding, source binding, ordered-execution binding, oracle separation, persisted-object replay, execution-rerun consistency, and version/access binding. Across 1,280 cross-object attacks, the joint contract detects 1,275 substitutions (0.9961). Removing a targeted property reduces its attack-detection rate to 0.0156-0.0625. On an independently adjudicated 384-pair split, the conflict-aware support guard reaches F1 0.8865 and false acceptance 0.0729; on unseen failure families, these rates are 0.8679 and 0.0938.

items.title: FAER: Auditable Utility-Aligned Trajectory Replay for Language Model Post-Training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: FAER: Auditable Utility-Aligned Trajectory Replay for Language Model Post-Training
items.summary: arXiv:2610.00385v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Replay selectors often rank cached trajectories by format feedback, confidence, freshness, or response length, although cache-level correctness and downstream learner utility are distinct objectives. We formalize this selection-to-learning gap and introduce FAER as an auditable full-trajectory replay framework. Its training-free fixed selector is a protocol baseline; FAER-UTILITY is the learner-aware selector fitted on disjoint calibration blocks. The normalized gradient alignment is reported as a baseline, while a disposable optimizer-aware virtual update supplies a magnitude-aware utility surface. The audit contract freezes observed fields and replay traces before evaluation labels are joined. On GSM8K with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, the matched learner study reports quality 0.6329 for the fixed selector, compared with 0.5482 for uniform and 0.6037 for format-feedback under 128 updates. Metadata-only cross-fitted calibration reaches $0.6476\!\pm\!0.0139$ over eight seeds (median 0.6481; paired 95% interval $[+0.079,+0.122]$) at 63,276 target-run tokens; its recorded full cost is 189,642 tokens and 3.48 GPU-hours including calibration. The completed FAER-UTILITY row reaches 0.6624 at 62,844 target-run tokens and 4.26 GPU-hours. Format-feedback selects records with correctness 0.6953, compared with 0.3594 for the fixed selector, despite the different downstream ranking. The completed comparison surfaces report the learner-aware ablation, same-seed gap, policy-optimization rows, and strict zero-shot transfer.

items.title: The Score Is Not the Structure: Brain Alignment and Cross-Lingual Transfer [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Score Is Not the Structure: Brain Alignment and Cross-Lingual Transfer
items.summary: arXiv:2610.03827v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Similarity scores are often offered as evidence that a model shares structure with the brain or across languages. We ask what such a score reads when that structure is removed, or when the instrument measuring it does not work, in two settings. Across seventeen languages, a grammaticality probe transfers worse between more distant languages (r = -0.66). But the probe's own accuracy falls along the same axis and is at chance in four languages, four of the five most distant. Dropping them halves the explained variance, and because it also narrows the range of distances, the design cannot say how much of the gradient is the instrument. items.title: PRIME: Towards Verifiable Evidence-Grounded Reasoning in LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: PRIME: Towards Verifiable Evidence-Grounded Reasoning in LLM Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.22426v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents are used to check records against an organization's requirements, for example whether a vulnerability report is ready for investigation. Requirements often allow several ways to be met, such as a severity rating with a curator-reviewed advisory or a published advisory link. Agents fail by accepting a report after a required check has failed, or by settling for a weaker conclusion without trying another way that could still succeed. We introduce PRIME (Precommitted Rules for Inference from Minimal Evidence). Before checking, it fixes evidence routes specifying how each conclusion may be justified. A separate program records each check result and refuses any conclusion the results do not justify. It also points the agent to checks that could justify a stronger conclusion, or runs them itself. PRIME reports only conclusions authorized by its rules and ledger. With correct requirements, exact checks at known locations, and sufficient budget at stopping, completion reaches the strongest supported conclusion. On 480 public-record tasks, an agent shown the requirements reported unjustified conclusions on 26.7% of tasks, while PRIME reported none. Its directions and added checks raised the average score for justified conclusions from 30.1, with refusal alone, to the maximum of 59.2 out of 100.

items.title: Null Controls Are Necessary but Not Sufficient: Evaluating Acceptance Guards for Scientific Discovery and Interpretability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Null Controls Are Necessary but Not Sufficient: Evaluating Acceptance Guards for Scientific Discovery and Interpretability
items.summary: arXiv:2610.22445v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated discovery systems propose scientific explanations and test which to accept. Does passing a test establish the intended claim? We develop four executable operations for changing physical descriptions: identifying redundancies (L1), coarse-graining dynamics (L2), transferring structure (L3), and inferring missing quantities from conservation imbalances (L4). We evaluate these operations and three interpretability settings through null acceptance (NAR), positive acceptance (PAR), and consequence agreement (CAR). A reduction mapping every state to zero predicts its own future perfectly. It passes closure on 96% of 129 public chaotic systems despite retaining no dynamical variation. An independent observable-preservation test rejects it throughout. On controlled benchmarks, the combined criteria accept 24/24 genuine reductions and reject 72/72 nulls. The other operations distinguish symmetries from redundancies, validate transfers, and reject spurious conservation imbalances. In language and ESM-2 protein models, linear CKA remains unchanged when a proposed correspondence is randomly rotated, whereas localized interventions distinguish genuine mappings from tested nulls. In sparse autoencoders, enrichment rejects all 16 tested nulls, yet independent ablation supports 45% of evaluable enriched features, compared with 0.5% of matched controls. These results reveal two acceptance gaps: descriptive tests can accept scientifically empty candidates, and accepted candidates can lack independently verified consequences. Reliable automated discovery requires evaluating both what a test accepts and the scientific consequences it establishes. Code and data: https://real-project-aether.github.io/project-aether/.

items.title: Learnable Splines for Unstructured Neural Operators [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Learnable Splines for Unstructured Neural Operators
items.summary: arXiv:2610.22446v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural operators approximate solution operators of partial differential equations at a fraction of the cost of numerical solvers. Efficient grid-based architectures such as the Fourier neural operator (FNO) assume uniform rectangular grids, whereas engineering simulations use large, irregular, and locally refined meshes. We introduce L-SplineFNO, a memory-efficient neural operator that couples an FNO backbone with a sparse, learnable tensor-product B-spline transfer between unstructured meshes and a latent Cartesian grid. A local normalised scatter avoids the geometry-dependent solve of analytic spline transformation while preserving compact support, partition of unity, and spline smoothness by construction. The neural operator, conditioned on global design and operating parameters, learns the mapping of geometry to the field solution. Across six three-dimensional engineering benchmarks, L-SplineFNO achieves strong predictive accuracy while requiring substantially less memory and compute than baseline operators, scaling to 26.6 million nodes in training and 46 million in inference on a single A100 GPU. It also supports zero-shot super-resolution and efficient closed-form spatial derivatives. Uniquely, the analytic spline decoder yields rigorous prediction bounds over continuous space and uncertain parameters, via Bernstein convex hulls and Taylor models, demonstrated on a 29.2-million-node MAST-U tokamak model.

items.title: Are Large Reasoning Models Good Everyday Reasoners? A Comparison with Non-Reasoning Models on Logical Reasoning Tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Are Large Reasoning Models Good Everyday Reasoners? A Comparison with Non-Reasoning Models on Logical Reasoning Tasks
items.summary: arXiv:2610.22538v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) that leverage test-time computation achieve strong performance on mathematical and scientific benchmarks and are increasingly deployed in real-world applications. However, their ability to perform \textit{everyday logical reasoning}, which often departs from textbook formal logic, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically evaluate how well reasoning models align with everyday reasoning patterns by introducing a benchmark based on linguistic and pragmatic reasoning phenomena. We also compare reasoning models with non-reasoning models under controlled prompting conditions. We find that, in many cases, (1) reasoning models show degraded performance in everyday reasoning when such reasoning deviates from formal logical rules, (2) some non-reasoning models with chain-of-thought prompting outperform comparable reasoning models in everyday reasoning, and (3) prompting with additional instructions provides limited control over reasoning behavior. These findings suggest that current reasoning models do not reliably capture everyday reasoning and point to limitations in post-training, motivating improved training objectives and evaluation across diverse forms of reasoning.

items.title: Repairing LLM-Generated Specifications with Deterministic Diagnosis [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Repairing LLM-Generated Specifications with Deterministic Diagnosis
items.summary: arXiv:2610.22568v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as formalizers: given a reasoning problem expressed in natural language, they produce a formal specification that a symbolic solver can then solve, with guarantees relative to that specification. Many specifications are runnable yet semantically wrong, encoding incorrect constraints, domains, objectives, predicates, or goals, and solver-error feedback dries up once execution succeeds. Purely LLM-based diagnosis, lacking a formal ground truth, often fails to spot these errors, and its ungrounded critiques cause regressions in 11.8% of initially correct specifications in our experiments. We propose DRAGO, a repair framework that replaces this ungrounded critique with deterministic, formalism-specific diagnosis, and retains a rewrite only when the diagnosed error weight strictly decreases under a reference-free acceptance predicate. Across five benchmarks spanning logical reasoning (SMT-LIB2), constraint programming (MiniZinc), and planning (PDDL), DRAGO cuts regressions by nearly an order of magnitude, to 1.3%, while improving answer accuracy by 12.9 percentage points over zero-shot formalization and 8.7 percentage points over LLM-diagnostic repair, averaged across benchmarks. We also uncover two rendering defects in Planetarium that cause 50% (3,086 instances) of its floor-tile split to be inconsistent with the reference formalizations, and release a corrected split.

items.title: Not All Graphs Are Maps: A Task-Agnostic Exploration Framework for Mobile GUI Navigation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Not All Graphs Are Maps: A Task-Agnostic Exploration Framework for Mobile GUI Navigation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.22672v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern mobile GUI agents can perceive visible screens and execute local actions, but they still lack persistent app-specific navigation knowledge: where functions live, which pages contain them, and which screens are equivalent across repeated visits. We introduce TAG-Nav, a Task-Agnostic Graph Navigation framework that wraps existing GUI-agent backbones with reusable destination memory. Offline exploration is distilled into compact records of app functions, target pages, and waypoint routes before any evaluated instruction is seen. When a future task's destination is covered, TAG-Nav retrieves the destination and provides route guidance without task-specific demonstrations. This separates mobile GUI destination navigation from full task completion: many tasks share the prefix of reaching the right page, while final actions may enter content, send data, make purchases, delete information, or change sensitive settings. To evaluate route finding without downstream execution confounds, we introduce DestBench, a navigation-only protocol that asks whether an agent reaches the correct pre-action destination screen. DestBench enables a controlled graph-memory study comparing no-memory agents with random, automated BFS, and clean graph memory. Graph-derived memory improves strict navigation success rate of UI-TARS-1.5-7B from 52.4% without graph memory to 58.3% with automated BFS memory, and improves Qwen-VL-Max success rate from 59.5% to 71.4% on the same conditions. Together, TAG-Nav and DestBench show that destination coverage and route cleanliness strongly shape graph-memory value, making graph quality a measured variable rather than an assumed benefit of exploration.

items.title: GlobeBench: Evaluating Text-Based World Model Capabilities for Scalable Environment Simulations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: GlobeBench: Evaluating Text-Based World Model Capabilities for Scalable Environment Simulations
items.summary: arXiv:2610.22708v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text-based world models have recently shown potential to simulate complex RL environment state transitions for a diverse set of use cases. However, no standardized benchmark exists to compare, study and improve these models. Through this paper, we attempt to solve this problem by building GlobeBench, a novel benchmark with 1,632 tasks across five separate domains and nineteen simulation skills. The tasks check whether models can predict the environment's response to a specific action given the full agent trajectory by understanding earlier state changes, following environment rules, and predicting the effects of actions on both related and unrelated objects. We compare the predicted environment response with an execution-derived reference, using a hybrid architecture with both deterministic gates and a semantic judge. Among 20 general-purpose LLMs and specialized text world models, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest task success rate at 49.57%. We find that model accuracy decreases as actions affect a larger portion of the environment. Specifically, when the agent's changes must propagate to dependent objects, task success drops to an average of 5.1% across all 20 models. Although model strengths differ across tasks, 631 tasks remain unsolved by any model, suggesting a significant gap in general LLM capabilities as a world model.

items.title: ToPA: Block-wise Toeplitz Adaptation for Expressive and Efficient Fine-Tuning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ToPA: Block-wise Toeplitz Adaptation for Expressive and Efficient Fine-Tuning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.22883v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) has emerged as a prevalent strategy for adapting large pre-trained models. Among PEFT techniques, reparameterization-based methods, particularly those that employ low-rank or sparsity structures, have attracted significant attention. However, these approaches often underperform full fine-tuning. Specifically, low-rank methods constrain the update rank, which is misaligned with the inherently high-rank nature of full fine-tuning. In contrast, sparsity-based techniques limit the flexibility of the parameter space and compromise connectivity across weights. To overcome these limitations, we explore the use of Toeplitz matrices, whose entries are constant along each diagonal, therefore providing a compact parameterization without imposing explicit rank or sparsity constraints. A straightforward approach is to update weights via a product of Toeplitz matrices. However, similar to RNNs, long multiplicative chains often lead to gradient instability. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{ToPA}, a more refined version of this idea that replaces standard Toeplitz matrices with block-wise Toeplitz, greatly increasing each factor's capacity and shortening the chain, thereby stabilizing training and improving expressiveness. We theoretically show that products of block-wise Toeplitz matrices can approximate arbitrary matrices under shorter chain length, justifying the structural design of ToPA. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ToPA offers greater expressivity than existing low-rank and sparse parameterizations. Empirical evaluations across 21 NLP and CV datasets, spanning 5 model architectures, consistently validate the effectiveness of ToPA.

items.title: When to Forget: Risk-Controlled Context Adaptation for Long-Horizon Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: When to Forget: Risk-Controlled Context Adaptation for Long-Horizon Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.22897v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon agents learn from failure, but the value of a failure record can change as execution progresses. We study when retaining, compressing, or removing the same history block improves subsequent execution relative to full-history KEEP. We introduce RECAP, a framework that combines matched context interventions, execution-relational prediction, and independent policy certification. Matched environment states and rollout seeds measure success and continuation prompt-cost differences; prefix-only relations between a failure block and the current execution propose promising edits. Independent task bundles then select a policy subject to harmful-intervention and non-positive-benefit risk constraints under a fixed measurement protocol. A five-seed longitudinal case holds both the failure block and its summary fixed: compression fails at an early state and becomes a cost-saving intervention at a later state. Across five backbones, RECAP produces positive paired-success saving estimates with backbone-specific reliability-efficiency tradeoffs. On Hunyuan-A13B, it edits 43.24% of retained checkpoints while matching KEEP's observed 91.89% continuation success and reducing unconditional mean continuation prompt cost by 4,619.8 tokens (2.13%). The framework provides an execution-level reference for deciding when to forget: retain history by its value to what comes next.

items.title: Sep-Latent: Separator Tokens as Natural Compression Anchors for Implicit Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Sep-Latent: Separator Tokens as Natural Compression Anchors for Implicit Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.22924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable success in complex reasoning through explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT), but the associated computational overhead and token verbosity remain significant barriers to efficiency. While implicit reasoning in continuous latent spaces offers a promising alternative, existing methods like Coconut and CODI often rely on fixed-length latent sequences and suffer from representational collapse. In this paper, we propose Sep-Latent, an adaptive implicit reasoning framework that utilizes separator tokens as structural semantic anchors. By introducing an Attention-Decay mechanism, we force the model to aggregate and compress reasoning logic into these anchors during training. We then align explicit and implicit pathways through multi-level distillation across all layers to ensure logical consistency. Crucially, Sep-Latent enables dynamic reasoning depth by adaptively terminating the latent thinking phase based on query complexity. Experimental results on the GSM8k-Aug benchmark show that Sep-Latent achieves an accuracy of 56.8\% with an average of only 5.4 tokens, significantly outperforming prior fixed-length implicit models in efficiency while narrowing the performance gap with explicit CoT. Further analysis via PCA and symbolic variant testing confirms that our method ensures semantic grounding and exhibits superior robustness to perturbations.
